name: virtual-proxy
intent: Stand in for an expensive-to-construct object and create the real object only on first use, so clients can hold, pass and wire references without paying construction cost until a use actually demands it.
problem: An object whose construction is expensive (decode, query, dial, allocate, load) is often referenced long before it is used, or never used at all. Eager construction makes every creator - and often application startup - pay the full cost, while the hand-rolled alternative (a nullable field checked and filled at each use site) duplicates the decision, spreads the construction policy across callers and races under concurrency.
context: Applies when construction is expensive and use is uncertain or late: wide object graphs loaded from a store (ORM associations), large media or documents in a UI, remote service stubs, reports, configuration and models. Two conditions shape the realization: access may be concurrent, so the deferral has to be single-flight or the construction idempotent, and consumers may observe identity or type (collections, serialization, instanceof, ORM session identity), so the stand-in must be transparent where it matters.
benefits: Never-used objects are never constructed: CPU, memory, I/O, network and credential cost is paid only when the object is actually touched.
Startup and first-response latency improve because expensive work moves off the critical path instead of being front-loaded into construction of a whole object graph.
The construction policy - arguments, caching, pooling, retry - lives in one place (the stand-in or its factory) instead of being repeated at every use site as a null check.
Transparent to clients: the stand-in satisfies the same interface, so existing call sites, collections and wiring keep working unchanged.
Composes with the other proxy intents: the same stand-in can defer construction and then also guard, cache, log, count references or protect access to the real subject.
Makes expensive objects first-class participants in structures (lists, trees, mappings) as cheap handles that materialize only when they become interesting.
Centralises diagnostics: whether the real object was ever materialized, and when, is observable in one place, so the deferral can be measured rather than assumed.
tradeoffs: The cost moves rather than disappears: every access pays an indirection and an initialization check - Scala compiles a per-val state check, and a volatile double-checked field is re-read on every access even after construction.

Failures surface late and in the wrong place: construction errors happen at first use, far from startup, and the caching policy decides whether they stick (C# caches the factory exception by default, C++ std::call_once retries after a throwing initializer).

Identity and type observations break: the stand-in is not the real object, so getClass/instanceof, equals/hashCode/toString, serialization and debuggers can see the proxy; ORM lazy proxies need explicit identity and detach/attach handling.

Concurrency is subtle: naive check-then-act builds the object twice, double-checked locking is broken without volatile/atomic publication, and a correct guard costs synchronization or an atomic read on the hot path.

Structural deadlocks are possible: guards that do not tolerate reentrancy hang when the initializer touches the same member (Go sync.Once, pthread_once, Rust OnceLock, Scala lazy vals locked through the instance monitor).

Lifetime is inverted: the stand-in keeps the real subject and its resources alive, and it can outlive the context that made construction legitimate (a database session), which forces inject/detach escape hatches.
Observability drops: members show up uninitialized in dumps, and a load triggered by an innocent property read is hard to attribute - the classic N+1 query storm from lazy ORM associations.

participants.responsibility: The interface shared by the stand-in and the real object, so a client can hold either without knowing which one it has.
Implements Subject, keeps only the cheap construction input (identifier, path, parameters, factory), forwards every request after ensuring the real subject exists, and caches it.
The expensive object that owns the actual behaviour; created on demand by the proxy and used unchanged afterwards.
Encapsulates everything construction needs - arguments, credentials, session, configuration - and is invoked exactly once by the guard.
Makes first access create the real subject exactly once under concurrent access, or defines what happens when threads race (duplicate construction, blocking, discarded losers).
Uses the stand-in through the Subject interface, never asks for construction explicitly, and is unaffected by when it happens.

use_cases: Object-relational mappings: an association stays a stand-in until a property (not the identifier) is read - Hibernate/JPA lazy proxies, EF Core lazy-loading proxies, SQLAlchemy lazy relationships.
Large media in a UI: an image, scene or embedded document object remembers its file and decodes on first draw, while layout uses cached metadata such as dimensions.
Expensive shared resources behind a cheap handle: a connection, parser, model or report is built on first use, with the construction parameters held by the stand-in.
Remote service access: the client stub resolves credentials or opens the connection on the first call instead of at construction or application start.
Startup-path object graphs: a container registers heavyweight components that must exist by name but may never be touched in a given run.
Test fixtures and doubles: an expensive fixture is materialized only in the tests that exercise it, keeping the rest of the suite cheap.

Front-end lazy components: React.lazy(() => import('./Heavy')) hands the tree a stand-in component that defers loading the module until the element first renders, suspends on a Suspense fallback, and caches the resolved module for later renders.

Container lazy resolution: Spring @Lazy on an injection point injects a lazy-resolution proxy that resolves the target bean on the first method call instead of at startup, so heavyweight singletons exist by name until touched.
avoid_when: Construction is cheap or the object is always used: build it directly - the indirection is pure overhead when there is no deferred cost to save.
Construction must fail fast: when a missing dependency should abort startup, initialize eagerly rather than discovering the failure at first use under load.
Creation must stay visible in the caller's control flow or transaction: hidden triggering turns a deliberate step into a side effect of property access.
A simpler mechanism covers the need: a lazy-initialization helper or construct-on-first-use for one member, lazy loading at the data-access boundary, or a plain factory call at the point of use.
Access is single-threaded and trivially guarded: a nullable field plus an if is clearer than a dedicated stand-in class.
The interface is a value or data-transfer object: value semantics (copy, equality, serialization) fight a stand-in that owns deferred state.
anti_patterns: "Lazy everything": marking every member lazy so no cost is ever paid up front, converting a targeted optimization into pervasive indirection.
A stand-in with broken identity: forwarding the work but not equals/hashCode/toString or type queries, so it misbehaves in sets, maps, assertions and serialization.

Silent failure caching or unbounded retry: the first failed construction is remembered forever (or retried on every access) without a documented policy, turning a transient fault into a permanent outage or a stampede.

Deferring the security decision together with the construction: moving a privileged object behind a stand-in without moving its authorization check, so the check happens late, on an unexpected thread, or not at all.
Re-implementing lazy proxies on top of a framework that already owns them (ORM fetch strategies, DI container lazy resolution, generated proxies).
Leaking the trigger to callers: clients calling initialize()/load() to make the stand-in usable, which defeats the transparency the pattern exists for.
design_principles: Defer work until it is needed: pay the construction cost only when a use actually demands the object.
Indirection and information hiding: the stand-in hides both the cost and the moment of construction from clients.
Single responsibility: the real subject owns behaviour, the stand-in owns the creation decision and its guard.
Substitutability: the stand-in must satisfy the same interface and the same observable contract, including identity-sensitive operations.
Make the failure policy explicit: state whether a failed construction is retried, cached or escalated, and where that happens.
best_practices: Keep the stand-in substitutable: same interface, same observable semantics, and explicit forwarding for equals/hashCode/toString wherever the language relies on them.
Use the runtime's single-flight primitive instead of hand-rolled double-checked locking (std::call_once, sync.Once, OnceLock, Lazy<T>, by lazy, lazy val).
Decide and document failure semantics - retry, cache, or fail fast - and keep retry logic inside the construction hook when a transient failure is possible.
Hold only cheap construction state in the stand-in (identifier, path, factory, parameters), never a second copy of the real object's data.
Make the deferral observable: log or meter the first initialization, and test both the never-initialized and the initialized path.
Do not run heavy work while holding a lock the initializer may need; prefer guards that tolerate reentrancy or fail loudly instead of deadlocking.
Handle the never-initialized case in lifecycle code (close, dispose, serialize, detach) instead of forcing construction just to shut down.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) - Proxy, pp. 207-217, application 'a virtual proxy creates expensive objects on demand' (ImageProxy example).
